title: Three Structural Signatures
takeaway: The J-space carries workspace-like content only in a middle band of layers, holds few concepts at a time there, and is wired for broadcast: the model's MLPs and a small set of attention heads distribute its contents far more widely than other directions. The figure is a stylized preview of these three structural claims, which section 4 then establishes by measurement.
walkthrough:
This is a schematic, not a data plot. It sits at the end of the introduction and previews the three structural findings of section 4 about the [[j-space]] — the region of activation space built from [[jacobian-lens]] vectors, one vector per vocabulary token per layer. Everything in it maps onto the grid used throughout the paper: layers of the [[residual-stream]] running bottom to top, token positions running left to right. Layer numbers are reported on a 0–100 scale, so a layer index reads as a percentage of the model's depth ([[layer-percentage-indexing]]).

The first property is a band in the layer direction ([[layer-bands]]). The J-space is defined at every layer, but it behaves like a workspace only in a middle range, roughly L38 to L92. Below the band, lens readouts are noisy and nearly empty; the paper calls these the sensory layers. Above it, readouts collapse onto the token the model is about to emit; these are the motor layers. In the illustration, the workspace is the horizontal stripe between the two.

The second property is limited capacity ([[j-space-capacity]]). Inside the band, a sparse decomposition of an activation finds only about 25 meaningfully active J-lens vectors in the median case, and those directions carry under 10% of activation variance beyond a random control. In functional terms the limit is tighter still: around six unrelated concepts across the band, and one or two at any single layer. The illustration renders this as a few occupied slots against a much larger representational space that stays outside the J-space.

The third property is broadcast ([[j-space-broadcast]]). A transformer moves information along two axes: down through layers at one position, and across positions through attention ([[two-time-dimensions]]). The model's weights favor J-space content on both. MLP blocks amplify J-lens directions roughly tenfold within the band, against near-unit gain for control directions, and a top-1% subset of attention heads — the [[broadcast-heads]] — selectively relays J-space content to later positions. The illustration draws this as a hub: arrows fanning out from workspace content to many downstream consumers.

The figure itself asserts nothing; it is a picture of claims defended later by measurements on weights and activations. The paper also states what the picture does not show: no encapsulated input modules, and broadcast that runs over the depth of a single forward pass rather than through recurrent loops.

terms.definition: The set of activation-space points expressible as sparse nonnegative combinations of J-lens vectors; the paper's candidate for a global workspace in the model. All three illustrated properties are properties of this object.

One direction in the residual stream per vocabulary token per layer, identified by the Jacobian lens as encoding the model's potential to verbalize that token now or later. The J-space is built from these vectors.
The middle band of layers, roughly L38 to L92 on the paper's 0–100 depth scale, where the J-space carries persistent abstract content distinct from both the input tokens and the imminent output.
Roughly the first third of the model's depth, below the workspace band, where J-lens readouts are noisy and the J-space carries essentially no meaningful content.
The final few layers, above the workspace band, where lens contents align with the token the model is about to produce rather than with intermediate computation.

The second illustrated property: at any position in the workspace band, only a small number of concepts occupy the J-space, and the occupied directions account for a small share of activation variance.

The third illustrated property: the model's weights are configured to distribute J-space content disproportionately widely, so that many downstream circuits can read it — the structural counterpart of global workspace theory's broadcast.

The top 1% of workspace-layer attention heads by two weight-based metrics, which selectively relay J-space content between token positions; ablating them degrades J-space contents while leaving most next-token behavior intact.
The feed-forward component in each transformer layer. In the depth direction of the broadcast property, MLP blocks amplify J-space-aligned directions about tenfold within the workspace band.
The transformer operation that lets a position retrieve information from earlier positions; the sequence direction of the broadcast property runs through a small subset of these heads.
The running per-position vector that layers read from and write to; the vertical axis of the illustration is depth through this stream, and the J-space is a region of it.
One of the two axes of the illustration and one of the transformer's two time dimensions: content written to the residual stream at a position is available to every later layer at that position.
The other axis: attention makes a representation at one position available to all later positions. Broadcast across tokens travels along this axis.
The paper samples 25 evenly spaced layers and reindexes them 0–100, so L38 means about 38% of the way through the model's depth and L92 about 92%.

numbers.meaning: The number of structural properties illustrated: a workspace layer band, limited capacity, and broadcast privilege. Section 4 documents exactly these three signatures.

The approximate start of the workspace band, about a third of the way through the model's depth. Four independent lens-derived statistics (next-token accuracy, readout kurtosis, top-1 autocorrelation, effective dimensionality) all shift near this layer.

The approximate end of the workspace band, shortly before the output. Past it, lens readouts jump into agreement with the model's next-token prediction, which the paper reads as motor rather than workspace representation.

Median J-space occupancy across the workspace band: the number of J-lens vectors meaningfully active in an activation, measured as the sparsity level at which sparse decomposition stops beating a same-size random control. The value varies across contexts.

The ceiling on excess variance explained: the top-occupancy J-lens vectors never account for more than 10% of activation variance beyond a random control, so most of what the activation encodes lies outside the J-space.
In the word-list experiment, the number of unrelated list words simultaneously present in the J-lens top-25 across the band; the count stays flat as the list grows, with older words dropping out.
The number of unrelated concepts encoded at a single workspace layer at one time, when the list analysis is repeated at one layer instead of taking the best rank over the whole band.
The fraction of workspace-layer attention heads designated broadcast heads, selected by combining a gain metric and a label-preservation metric on each head's OV weights.

The approximate MLP gain on J-lens vectors in the workspace band: the next layer's MLP block amplifies them about ten times more than isotropic random directions, while control directions such as MLP neuron outputs stay near gain 1.

Recall@25 of J-lens readout tokens at the most affected mid-workspace layers after ablating the broadcast heads, versus after ablating equal-sized random head sets — evidence that these heads specifically carry J-space content.
